verses.text: The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw:
Set up a banner on the bare mountain! Lift up your voice to them! Wave your hand, that they may go into the gates of the nobles.
I have commanded my consecrated ones; yes, I have called my mighty men for my anger, even my proudly exulting ones.
The noise of a multitude is in the mountains, as of a great people; the noise of an uproar of the kingdoms of the nations gathered together! Yahweh of Armies is mustering the army for the battle.
They come from a far country, from the uttermost part of heaven, even Yahweh, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land.
Wail; for the day of Yahweh is at hand! It will come as destruction from the Almighty.
Therefore all hands will be feeble, and everyone’s heart will melt.
They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame.
Behold, the day of Yahweh comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger; to make the land a desolation, and to destroy its sinners out of it.
For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.
I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity. I will cause the arrogance of the proud to cease, and will humble the haughtiness of the terrible.
I will make people more rare than fine gold, even a person than the pure gold of Ophir.
Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place in Yahweh of Armies’ wrath, and in the day of his fierce anger.
It will happen that like a hunted gazelle, and like sheep that no one gathers, they will each turn to their own people, and will each flee to their own land.
Everyone who is found will be thrust through. Everyone who is captured will fall by the sword.
Their infants also will be dashed in pieces before their eyes. Their houses will be ransacked, and their wives raped.
Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, who will not value silver, and as for gold, they will not delight in it.
Their bows will dash the young men in pieces; and they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb. Their eyes will not spare children.
Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldeans’ pride, will be like when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.
It will never be inhabited, neither will it be lived in from generation to generation. The Arabian will not pitch a tent there, neither will shepherds make their flocks lie down there.
But wild animals of the desert will lie there, and their houses will be full of jackals. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will frolic there.
Wolves will cry in their fortresses, and jackals in the pleasant palaces. Her time is near to come, and her days will not be prolonged.

footnotes.content: Isaiah sees the burden—the weight—of Babylon's coming judgment. A burden is something you must carry and deliver, not merely speak about. Notice how the prophet names both the city and himself: a message belongs to a messenger, someone willing to bear it faithfully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The banner on the bare mountain speaks plainly where all can see it. This is Isaiah calling the nations to witness what God is doing. There's an honesty here—no hiding the message, no private warning. The nobles must know that judgment comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God speaks of His 'consecrated ones' and 'mighty men'—soldiers chosen for this work. In scripture, 'consecrated' usually means set apart for holiness, yet here it refers to instruments of divine wrath. It's a sober reminder that God's purposes use human hands, even in judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Picture the sound: mountains roaring with the movement of many peoples and armies. Yahweh of Armies is mustering—not just watching, but actively gathering the forces. When God Himself orders the nations, the earth trembles with it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They come 'from a far country, from the uttermost part of heaven'—the image is of Yahweh's hand reaching across the whole earth to fetch judgment. These are not random invaders but God's instruments, His weapons of indignation, to destroy the whole land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wail—the prophet calls the people to grieve. The day of Yahweh is at hand, bringing destruction from the Almighty. There's a pastoral clarity here: this is not distant theology but present reality pressing in. Weeping is the only honest response.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Feeble hands and melting hearts describe the inner collapse that terror brings. Isaiah doesn't detail the blood and fire of war—he shows what happens inside us when we meet the living God in judgment. Weakness and fear are the natural fruit of resistance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Like a woman in labor—one of scripture's truest comparisons for distress without relief. Their faces become 'faces of flame,' burning with terror and shame. The imagery traces the path from panic to horror to utter helplessness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The day of Yahweh is described as cruel, with wrath and fierce anger—not abstract, but actively destructive. Notice the purpose: to destroy the sinners 'out of' the land. Judgment is surgical, not random; it targets rebellion, not the land itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sun darkened, the moon refusing its light—Isaiah uses the language of deep cosmic disorientation. In every ancient culture, the stars gave order and meaning to night. Their failure speaks of a world unmade, a hierarchy shattered. Only the God who hung them can darken them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their iniquity—simple, direct justice. Then He humbles the proud and terrible, those who lifted themselves high. There's mercy in it: He stops the arrogance that would destroy others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: People rarer than fine gold, rarer than Ophir's finest—the image of massive death and desolation. What was abundant becomes scarce. In one verse, the prophet conveys a whole empire laid waste, reduced to fragments.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will make the heavens tremble and shake the earth—Yahweh Himself is the agent, and His wrath shakes creation. The cosmic and earthly join in a single tremor. This is not a local war but a confrontation of the whole universe with its God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Like hunted gazelles with no shepherd to gather them—each person flees alone to their own people, their own land. The picture is not of armies but of families scattered, the social order shattered. Isolation follows judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Everyone found is thrust through; everyone captured falls by the sword. The brutality is plain and not softened. Yet notice: Isaiah does not glory in it. He reports it as the straightforward outcome of rebellion against God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The worst cruelties—infants dashed, houses ransacked, women violated—are the bitter fruit when a nation hardens itself against God. Isaiah speaks plainly of what conquerors do. It's not punishment God inflicts but the evil that men bring on each other when they turn from Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Medes are stirred up against Babylon—ruthless, unmoved by silver or gold. Historically, Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians. What greed cannot move, God moves. The nations are instruments in His hand, not masters of their own course.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bows dashing young men, no pity on the unborn, eyes not sparing children—the Medes spare nothing and no one. It's the harvest of Babylon's own violence and pride. A nation that built its power on cruelty finds cruelty returned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, is likened to Sodom and Gomorrah. Both were cities of terrible pride and unrepentant sin; both fell under fire from heaven. The parallel is exact: when God judges, even glory cannot stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Never inhabited from generation to generation—the city dies, its purpose finished. Nomads won't pitch tents there; shepherds won't bring their flocks. A once-great place becomes empty, forsaken, a monument to what pride brings forth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wild animals and jackals fill the houses, and ostriches frolic where once the proud strutted. The irony is gentle and complete: human glory empties, and the wilderness reclaims what men built. Creation itself reverses their work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wolves cry in fortresses, jackals in palaces—readers today hear an echo in every empire that seemed eternal and then crumbled to dust. We see it still: great powers humbled, cities abandoned, pride brought low. The pattern holds because God's justice doesn't change.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
